key_terms.meaning: The smallest set of present-day variables whose values, together with future inputs, completely fix the future behaviour of the system
One of the n variables (capacitor voltage, position, velocity, current) that together describe the system's present condition
Column vector x = [x₁ x₂ … xₙ]ᵀ collecting all n state variables at time t
Number of independent state variables; equals the number of energy-storage elements and the degree of the denominator of the transfer function
The pair of first-order matrix equations ẋ = Ax + Bu and y = Cx + Du
Gives how the states drive each other when the input is zero
Gives how each of the m inputs enters the n state equations
Gives how the states are combined to form the p outputs
Feedthrough from input to output with no state delay; it is zero when the transfer function is strictly proper
y = Cx + Du, an algebraic (not differential) relation between states, input and output
State model in which A is the companion matrix of the denominator coefficients and B = [0 … 0 1]ᵀ
Dual of the controllable form: A is in companion form and C = [0 … 0 1]
G(s) = C(sI − A)⁻¹B + D; each term is a p × m matrix
Φ(t) = e^{At}; it carries the state from x(0) to x(t) when the input is zero
Σ from k = 0 to ∞ of Aᵏtᵏ/k!, defined for every square matrix A
Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation; it lets e^{At} be written as a finite polynomial in A
Q_c = [B AB A²B … Aⁿ⁻¹B]; the system is controllable if and only if rank Q_c = n
Q_o = [C; CA; CA²; …; CAⁿ⁻¹] stacked as rows; observable if and only if rank Q_o = n
Control law u = −Kx + r gives closed-loop matrix A − BK, whose eigenvalues are the new poles
K = [0 0 … 1] Q_c⁻¹ φ(A), where φ(A) is the desired closed-loop characteristic polynomial evaluated at A

takeaways: A state model replaces one nth-order differential equation with n first-order equations written as ẋ = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du.
The order n equals the number of independent energy-storage elements; for a transfer function it is the degree of the denominator.
The poles of the system are the eigenvalues of A, found from det(sI − A) = 0.
Any transfer function can be turned into a state model in controllable, observable or diagonal canonical form, and the choice is yours.
The reverse trip uses G(s) = C(sI − A)⁻¹B + D, which must reduce to the original transfer function.
The free response is x(t) = e^{At}x(0), so the whole behaviour of the system sits inside the state transition matrix.
Controllability is a rank test on [B AB … Aⁿ⁻¹B]; observability is a rank test on the stacked CAⁱ rows.
A pole-zero cancellation in G(s) makes that mode either uncontrollable or unobservable, even though the transfer function looks innocent.
Pole placement by state feedback works exactly when the system is controllable, and the gain is found from Ackermann's formula or by matching coefficients.
bank_note: Long answers here are usually half derivation and half numerical: define the state model, convert between transfer function and state space in a named canonical form, solve ẋ = Ax for x(t), run the rank tests, then place poles with state feedback.

bank.q: Define state, state variable and state vector. Write the general state model of a linear time-invariant system with m inputs and p outputs, and explain the size and meaning of each matrix.
outline: State = least set of present variables that fixes the future with future inputs
ẋ = Ax + Bu with A n × n, B n × m, x n × 1
y = Cx + Du with C p × n, D p × m
Order n = number of independent storage elements
D is zero when the transfer function is strictly proper
One worked example: RLC series circuit or mass-spring-damper with x₁ = displacement, x₂ = velocity

bank.q: Explain the controllable canonical form, the observable canonical form and the diagonal (Jordan) canonical form of a state model, using a third-order transfer function as the example.
outline: Controllable form: A companion matrix of denominator coefficients, B = [0 0 1]ᵀ, C from numerator coefficients
Observable form: transpose/dual arrangement, C = [0 0 1]
Diagonal form needs distinct real poles; residues give C and B
Repeated poles give a Jordan block
Statement that all three represent the same transfer function

bank.q: Derive the expression G(s) = C(sI − A)⁻¹B + D for the transfer function of a state model, starting from the Laplace transform of the state equations.
outline: Take Laplace with zero initial conditions: sX(s) = AX(s) + BU(s)
(sI − A)X(s) = BU(s) so X(s) = (sI − A)⁻¹BU(s)
Y(s) = CX(s) + DU(s)
Hence G(s) = C(sI − A)⁻¹B + D
det(sI − A) is the denominator, so poles are eigenvalues of A
Note that the formula holds for multi-input multi-output systems as a matrix

bank.q: Define the state transition matrix and list its properties, proving any three of them.
outline: Φ(t) = e^{At}
Φ(t₁ + t₂) = Φ(t₁)Φ(t₂) and Φ⁻¹(t) = Φ(−t)
dΦ/dt = AΦ = ΦA
Φ(t) is nonsingular for all finite t
Columns of Φ(t) are the zero-input responses from unit initial states

bank.q: A system has transfer function Y(s)/U(s) = (2s + 3)/(s³ + 4s² + 5s + 6). Obtain a state model in controllable canonical form, then in observable canonical form.
outline: Observable: transpose structure with C = [0,0,1] and B = [3,2,0]ᵀ
Check both give the same transfer function
State clearly that many state models exist for one transfer function

bank.q: For A = [[0, 1], [−2, −3]] and B = [0, 1]ᵀ, compute e^{At} using the Cayley–Hamilton theorem and hence write the zero-input response for x(0) = [1, 0]ᵀ.
outline: Characteristic equation s² + 3s + 2 = 0, roots −1 and −2
Write e^{At} = α₀I + α₁A
Solve α₀ + α₁(−1) = e^{−t} and α₀ + α₁(−2) = e^{−2t}
Substitute back and multiply by x(0)
State that eigenvalues of A are the system poles

bank.q: Solve the state equation ẋ = Ax + Bu for a given 2 × 2 A, a constant input u(t) = 1 and x(0) = 0, using the convolution form of the solution.
outline: x(t) = e^{At}x(0) + ∫₀ᵗ e^{A(t−τ)}Bu(τ)dτ
Compute e^{At} first (Cayley–Hamilton or Laplace transform)
Set x(0) = 0 and u = 1
Integrate term by term with the correct limits
Check the answer against the steady-state value −A⁻¹B

bank.q: Test the following system for controllability and observability: A = [[1, 2], [0, 3]], B = [1, 1]ᵀ, C = [1, 0]. Interpret the result physically.
outline: Form Q_c = [B AB] and find its determinant
Form Q_o = [C; CA] and find its determinant
Rank test against n = 2
State clearly: controllable if rank Q_c = 2, observable if rank Q_o = 2
Interpret which mode is hidden and why

bank.q: A system with A = [[0, 1], [−2, −3]] and B = [0, 1]ᵀ is to have closed-loop poles at −5 and −5. Find the state feedback gain K using Ackermann's formula and verify the result.
outline: Verify controllability: rank [B AB] = 2
Desired polynomial φ(s) = s² + 10s + 25
Compute φ(A) = A² + 10A + 25I
K = [0 1]Q_c⁻¹φ(A)
Verify eigenvalues of A − BK are −5, −5
Note the control law is u = −Kx + r

bank.q: A transfer function shows a pole-zero cancellation. Explain, using the controllability and observability matrices, why the cancelled mode may be uncontrollable or unobservable, and what this means for the physical system.
outline: Cancelled mode is an eigenvalue of A but not a pole of G(s)
It appears in neither the controllable nor the observable part of the minimal realisation
Rank test fails in the corresponding canonical form
The hidden mode can still be excited by initial conditions
Consequence: a stable-looking transfer function may hide an unstable internal mode
State space separates what the transfer function mixes together

bank.q: Compare the transfer function approach and the state space approach for modelling and analysing control systems, giving at least four points of difference and one situation where each is preferred.
outline: Transfer function: single input single output, zero initial conditions, frequency domain
State space: multi-input multi-output, non-zero initial conditions, time domain
State space handles internal descriptions and hidden modes
Order and realisation not unique in state space
Hardware: transfer function suits classical design, state space suits computer control and modern design
Initial condition response is natural in state space but awkward in transfer functions

bank.q: Explain the conditions under which pole placement by state feedback is possible, and discuss two practical difficulties that appear when the theory is applied to a real plant.
outline: Necessary and sufficient condition: complete controllability, rank Q_c = n
Gain computed from Ackermann's formula or by coefficient matching
Difficulty 1: not all states are measurable, so an observer is needed
Difficulty 2: large gains demand large control effort and amplify noise
Effect of saturation and actuator limits
Pole choice trade-off between speed and effort

bank.q: For the armature-controlled DC motor or the series RLC circuit: build the state model from physical laws, find its transfer function, check controllability and observability, and design a state feedback gain that places both poles at a chosen location.
outline: Choose state variables: current and speed, or capacitor voltage and inductor current
Write the two first-order equations from Kirchhoff's or Newton's laws
Assemble A, B, C, D and state the order
Compute G(s) = C(sI − A)⁻¹B and check it against the known result
Form Q_c and Q_o and take ranks
Apply Ackermann's formula for the chosen poles
Comment on the physical meaning of the feedback gains

glossary.def: The least collection of present variables that, with future inputs, determines all future behaviour of the system.
Any one member of the set of n variables that describe the present condition of the system.
A column vector containing all n state variables at a given instant.
The n-dimensional space in which every possible state vector is one point.
The number of independent state variables, equal to the number of storage elements.
ẋ = Ax + Bu, the set of first-order differential equations in matrix form.
y = Cx + Du, relating the output algebraically to state and input.
The n × n matrix in the state equation that fixes the internal dynamics.
The n × m matrix that shows how the inputs enter the state equations.
The p × n matrix that shows how the states produce the outputs.
The p × m matrix giving the instantaneous input-to-output path; zero for strictly proper systems.
A standard, fixed pattern of A, B, C that represents a given transfer function.
A matrix whose last row (or column) holds the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial.
det(sI − A), whose roots are the eigenvalues of A and hence the system poles.
A scalar λ with Av = λv for some nonzero vector v; here the same as a system pole.
A state model of smallest possible order for a given transfer function, with no hidden modes.
e^{At}, the matrix that propagates the state forward in time under zero input.
The infinite series Σ Aᵏtᵏ/k!, the matrix version of e^{at}.
Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation, allowing powers of A to be reduced.
The property that some input can drive the state from any initial value to any final value in finite time.
The property that the output over finite time is enough to determine the initial state.
Choosing feedback gains so that the closed-loop eigenvalues sit at desired locations.
A control law u = −Kx + r that uses all state variables, not just the output.
K = [0 … 0 1]Q_c⁻¹φ(A), a direct way to compute the state feedback gain.
A software or hardware estimator that reconstructs unmeasured states from input and output.
